task: Have adops init generate GitHub Actions workflows: on PR open or update, run adops validate and adops run --branch; on PR merge or close, run adops drop-branch; on merge to main, run stage; on release, run prod. Settle first how CI reaches the stage Warehouse, the policy for PRs from forks, and how to stop branch and stage runs from overlapping.

analysis.objective: Make `adops init` (plain and --demo) generate GitHub Actions workflows that deliver GitOps Promotion: a PR runs `adops validate` plus `adops run --all --branch` on the stage Server's self-hosted runner (only validate, with no secrets, for a Fork PR); closing or merging a PR runs `adops drop-branch`; a merge to main checks out the merged commit in the stage Server's Project folder and runs validate plus `adops run --all --env stage`; a release does the same on the prod Server behind an approved GitHub `prod` environment. Overlapping runs are prevented by a new Warehouse lock that adops itself takes, and the CI-reach and Fork PR policy are recorded in new ADRs.
analysis.successDefinition: Done when ALL hold, with 100% line+branch coverage on adops package code and the repo gates (uv sync --locked, ruff, pytest, the template-in-wheel check, the Docker E2E within its 20-minute limit) green: (1) `adops init` and `adops init --demo` write workflow files under .github/workflows/ (exact file set asserted by test_init_command; no *.py written, per ADR-0008), and every generated file is listed in the CI template-in-wheel check. (2) Unit tests parse each generated workflow and assert its triggers, jobs and steps: pull_request opened/synchronize/reopened, where a Fork PR runs only `adops validate` on a GitHub-hosted runner with no secrets and prints a plain skip message, while a same-repo PR runs `adops validate` then `adops run --all --branch <head branch>` on the runner labelled for stage; pull_request closed (same-repo only) runs `adops drop-branch <head branch>` on the stage runner; push to main updates the stage Server's Project folder to the merged commit, then runs `adops validate` and then `adops run --all --env stage`; release published runs the same steps on the runner labelled for prod with `environment: prod`, checking out the release tag. No workflow puts a Warehouse or Source secret in GitHub secrets. adops is installed at the pinned version from the same spec the Server Dockerfile uses. (3) `adops run --all` runs every Pipeline in name order, stops at the first failure with a non-zero exit, works with --env and with --branch, and exits with a clear error when combined with a Pipeline name or when there are no Pipelines; unit tested. (4) A Warehouse lock is taken by every run that touches a Warehouse: adops run (stage, prod, --branch), adops drop-branch, and Server scheduled runs. Postgres advisory lock on Postgres, an OS file lock beside the DuckDB file on DuckDB, waits up to a set timeout, then fails with a clear sanitized error. Unit tests cover acquire, wait, timeout and release-on-failure for both kinds, and an E2E case on both Warehouse kinds shows two overlapping runs are serialized. (5) A new ADR records the self-hosted runner on each Server machine, the Fork PR policy and the push of versions to the Server's Project folder; ADR-0014 and ADR-0006 get dated clarifications. (6) The demo and plain adops.yaml templates ship a commented prod Environment block, and a README/playbook section tells the user how to register the self-hosted runner with the stage/prod labels, create the GitHub `prod` environment with required reviewers, and keep 'require approval for fork PR workflows' on.

The scope answers in scope-answers.md are binding and replace the horizon-8 brief's Git-pull Server and ADR-0015 record work.

Each Server machine has one self-hosted runner, labelled `adops-stage` or `adops-prod`, running jobs on the host. The Server's Project folder is a Git checkout the runner can fetch into; .env and .adops/ are untracked and survive a checkout.

Warehouse-touching workflow steps run adops inside the Server image via docker compose run with the Server's .env loaded, so the same localhost adops.yaml reaches the Warehouse, as horizon 7 used network_mode: host.

adops is not on PyPI. Workflows install adops from one pinned package spec (same idea as the Server Dockerfile's ADOPS_PACKAGE/ADOPS_VERSION, defaulting to the generating adops __version__). No tool code is copied into the Project.
Merge to main runs every Pipeline (`--all`), not only changed ones, keeping stage's fingerprints current; closes the horizon-6 'changed-only' blocker by choice.

`adops run --all --branch <b>` defers unchanged Steps to stage per Pipeline exactly as `--branch` does today; the branch name comes from github.head_ref and is sanitized by the existing Branch name rule.
One self-hosted runner per Server runs one job at a time. The Warehouse lock is still required because the Server's Dagster schedule and the runner share the Warehouse.

The lock is taken around the whole Pipeline run, in one place reused by `adops run`, `drop-branch` and the Server's Dagster job. Postgres: session-level advisory lock on a dedicated connection. DuckDB: OS file lock on `<warehouse path>.lock`. Fixed default timeout (e.g. 30 minutes).
GitHub workflow behaviour itself is verified by asserting on the generated YAML, not by running GitHub Actions. The E2E proves the command sequence each workflow runs against the Docker stack.
A Breaking Change during a PR branch run fails the job with the existing sanitized error, fixed by hand (horizon-6 decision).
risks: Decision conflict: ADR-0014 rejected a self-hosted runner on the Server and chose Git polling. The user's scope answers reverse both; must be recorded as a new ADR plus a dated ADR-0014 clarification, not done silently.

Security: the `if: not fork` job condition is not a security boundary because a fork can edit the workflow file. Safety depends on GitHub's 'require approval for fork PR workflows' setting and trusting collaborators; adops cannot enforce this, so ADR and playbook must say so plainly, naming GitHub's guidance against self-hosted runners on public repos.

Updating the Server's Project folder from a workflow can fail or corrupt state: local edits, a checkout while a scheduled run reads files, untracked .env/.adops clobbered, or the running Dagster code location not picking up new definitions without a reload.
If `adops validate` fails after checkout, the folder is left on a bad version unless the workflow rolls back to the last good commit.
The Postgres advisory lock is per session; Dagster Server runs execute in a separate run process, so the lock must be taken inside the run, not in the daemon.
DuckDB lock file: runner host and Server container must see the same path through the bind mount; a stale lock after a crash must not block forever (use flock, not file existence).
A long PR branch run holding the lock can delay scheduled runs, and a Dagster run waiting on the lock holds the only run slot.
drop-branch on PR close races with the stage run and any in-flight branch run; GitHub cancel-in-progress could leave a half-built Branch Environment.
Short branch names can sanitize to the same Branch Environment, so drop-branch for one PR can drop another PR's schemas.
Installing a pinned adops on the runner without PyPI needs a reachable wheel or Git URL source; a wrong spec makes every workflow fail before adops runs.
The prod path is checked only through the generated YAML, so a runtime bug on prod goes unseen until a user's first release.
Adding workflow files changes the exact init file-set tests, the template-in-wheel grep and the .env.example coverage test, so those guards must be updated in the same phase.
outOfScope: The Git-pull Server from the horizon-8 brief (polling, Git credentials, latest-tag rule, hot-swap): replaced by the workflow pushing the version to the Server's Project folder.
ADR-0015 accepted-change records and changing `accept-schema` for stage/prod: a separate horizon.
`accept-schema --branch` and unattended handling of a Breaking Change in a PR branch: the horizon-6 gap stays recorded.
Merge→stage running only changed Pipelines: `--all` was chosen.
Automatically registering the self-hosted runner, creating the GitHub `prod` environment, or changing GitHub repo settings: need repo-admin credentials; documented as manual steps.
A live end-to-end run of the release→prod workflow or of GitHub Actions itself: prod is tested by checking the generated workflow file.
Reaching a Warehouse from GitHub-hosted runners (tunnels, cloud Warehouses, GitHub secrets for Warehouse credentials): rejected in favour of the self-hosted runner.
Publishing adops to PyPI: workflows use a pinned package spec.
The MCP server, the six skills and the Assistant opening PRs: later horizons.
Server run monitoring for runs left STARTED after a crash (horizon-7 blocker): separate.
Parallel or Step-graph execution, and locks for dev Warehouses: Steps stay linear.
The full single-VM production playbook (vision item 11): only the runner, fork-approval and prod-environment setup notes are written here.
analysis.domainShapeReason: The work is CI/CD machinery: generated workflow files, a self-hosted runner, a run lock and an `--all` flag. The Promotion rules it serves are already decided, and no new domain rule is modelled.

ubiquitousLanguage.meaning: Moving a Project version forward through Git: a PR runs a Branch Environment, a merge to main deploys to stage, and a published release deploys to prod after approval.

The GitHub Actions runner installed on a Server machine and labelled for stage or prod; it runs Warehouse-touching jobs with that machine's .env.
A pull request whose head repository differs from the base repository; it gets only `adops validate` on a GitHub-hosted runner with no secrets.

The Git checkout on a Server machine that the horizon-7 Server bind-mounts; merge and release workflows update it before running.
The lock adops takes for each run that touches a Warehouse; a second run waits, up to a timeout, instead of overlapping.

phases.name: Add --all option to adops run
phases.goal: `adops run --all` runs every Pipeline in the Project in name order and stops with a non-zero exit at the first failure. It works with --env and with --branch, so each generated workflow step can be one plain line.
phases.rationale: Every generated workflow has to run all Pipelines, and putting a shell loop in each workflow file would leave that logic untested. A single flag keeps the workflows short, and the logic is unit-tested at 100% coverage.
changes: Change run()'s positional `pipeline` (run_command.py:182) to `str | None = None` and add an `--all` bool option with help text 'Run every Pipeline in name order; stop at the first failure.'
Reject a Pipeline name together with --all, and reject neither of them, with typer.BadParameter and a plain message. Keep the existing --env/--branch conflict check as it is.

When --all is set, list pipelines/*.yaml sorted by name (the same rule server._pipelines uses at server.py:66-68). Exit 1 with 'No Pipelines in pipelines/' when there are none. Call run_project for each Pipeline in turn, print each result as today, and stop at the first failed result, exiting through fail().
Pass --env or --branch through unchanged to every run_project call, so `--all --branch <b>` keeps deferring unchanged Steps to stage for each Pipeline exactly as `--branch` does now.

Add unit tests for: name order, stop at the first failure (later Pipelines are not run), --all with --env, --all with --branch, name plus --all rejected, neither given rejected, and an empty pipelines/ folder. Update the CLI help tests in test_cli.py.
phases.expectedResult: `adops run --all [--env X | --branch B]` runs every Pipeline in name order and stops at the first failure, covered by unit tests at 100% line and branch coverage.
guardNotes: g1: new code is ruff clean (line length 100, import order).
g2: every new branch (both/neither given, empty folder, first-failure stop) has a unit test, so coverage stays at 100% with no exclusions.
g7: no pragma: no cover. Error output still goes through the existing error_lines/fail helpers, which redact secrets.

rubric.label: Name order and stop at first failure

phases.name: Add Warehouse lock for Postgres and DuckDB
phases.goal: Add one infrastructure module that holds an exclusive Warehouse lock for the length of a `with` block. On Postgres it is a session-level advisory lock on its own connection. On DuckDB it is an OS file lock (fcntl.flock) on '<warehouse file>.lock'. It waits up to a timeout, then raises a sanitized WarehouseLocked error.
phases.rationale: Today nothing stops a PR branch run, a stage run and a Server scheduled run from writing to the stage Warehouse at the same time, and DuckDB only allows one writer. This phase builds the lock mechanism by itself so its acquire, wait, timeout and release behaviour can be tested before anything relies on it. The repo has no file-lock code yet.
changes: Add a `WarehouseLocked` exception to application/ports.py next to WarehouseUnreachable (ports.py:52). Its message names only the Environment and the wait time, never a DSN or file path. It uses stdlib only.

Create infrastructure/warehouse_lock.py with a context manager `warehouse_lock(warehouse: ResolvedWarehouse, project_dir, environment, timeout=DEFAULT_LOCK_TIMEOUT, poll=..., sleep=time.sleep, monotonic=time.monotonic)`. It chooses the lock kind from ResolvedConnection versus ResolvedDuckDb. DEFAULT_LOCK_TIMEOUT is a fixed 30 minutes, with no env var or flag.

Postgres: open a dedicated autocommit psycopg connection from the ResolvedConnection fields, the same way postgres_reverse_sync._connected does. Poll `pg_try_advisory_lock(<fixed adops key>)` until it succeeds or the timeout passes. On exit, unlock and close in a finally block. Map psycopg.Error to WarehouseUnreachable without the DSN.

DuckDB: resolve the path with dlt_sync.duckdb_file(project_dir, path) and append '.lock'. Create the parent folder if it is missing, open the file and poll fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB) until the timeout. Release it in a finally block. Because flock belongs to the open file, a lock held by a process that crashed clears by itself, so the code does not check whether the file exists.

phases.name: Add generated pull request workflow to adops init
phases.goal: `adops init` and `adops init --demo` write .github/workflows/adops-pull-request.yml. For a same-repo PR it runs `adops validate` and `adops run --all --branch <head branch>` inside the Server image on the self-hosted runner labelled adops-stage, which is a GitHub Actions runner installed on the stage Server machine. When the PR is closed or merged, it runs `adops drop-branch <head branch>` there.
phases.rationale: A PR needs to build its Branch Environment (its own schemas in the stage Warehouse) and remove it on close, without stage secrets ever going into GitHub. Running these jobs on a runner on the stage Server machine reaches a localhost Postgres or DuckDB file Warehouse with that machine's .env. This phase also adds the shared workflow-writing code to init.

phases.name: Add generated stage and prod deploy workflows
phases.goal: `adops init` also writes adops-stage.yml (push to main) and adops-prod.yml (release published). Each runs on its Server's self-hosted runner and follows the same order: validate the runner's fresh checkout; only then move the Server Project folder (the folder the Server bind-mounts) to that commit or tag; ask the Server's Dagster to reload its code location; run `adops run --all --env stage|prod` inside the Server image. The prod job sits behind a GitHub `prod` environment that needs reviewer approval. The adops.yaml templates gain a commented prod Environment block.
phases.rationale: Merging to main must deploy to stage, and a release must deploy to prod after approval. The workflow pushes the new version to the Server instead of the Server polling Git, so no Git credentials or polling loop are needed. Validating before touching the Server folder means a bad version never replaces the running one, and reloading the code location (not restarting containers) lets an in-progress run finish on the old version.
changes: Write adops-stage.yml with `on: push: branches [main]`, runs-on [self-hosted, adops-stage], `permissions: contents: read`, `concurrency: group adops-stage, cancel-in-progress: false`, and the SHA-pinned checkout with fetch-depth: 0.

Step 1: run `adops validate` inside the Server image against the runner's checkout (the same docker compose run pattern as the PR workflow). If it fails, the job stops and the Server folder is left untouched.

Step 2: move the Server Project folder with `git -C "$ADOPS_SERVER_DIR" fetch "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE" "$GITHUB_SHA"` and `git -C "$ADOPS_SERVER_DIR" checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD`. This is a local fetch, so no Git credentials are needed, and the gitignored .env and .adops/ are not touched.

Step 3: reload Dagster with curl --fail POST to http://127.0.0.1:<DAGSTER_WEBSERVER_PORT>/graphql using the `reloadRepositoryLocation(repositoryLocationName: "adops.interface.server")` mutation (dagster-graphql 1.13.30; the location name is the python_module in workspace.yaml). Query `__typename` and, on WorkspaceLocationEntry, `loadStatus` and `locationOrLoadError { __typename }`. Read the port from the Server's .env with grep and do not source the file. Fail the step unless the response has __typename WorkspaceLocationEntry, loadStatus LOADED and locationOrLoadError.__typename RepositoryLocation; HTTP 200 alone, a PythonError location or a RepositoryLocationNotFound/UnauthorizedError union member is a failure. Step 4: `adops run --all --env stage` inside the Server image with the normal Server folder mount.

Write adops-prod.yml with the same four steps: `on: release: types [published]`, runs-on [self-hosted, adops-prod], `environment: prod`, checkout of the release tag (github.event.release.tag_name, passed through env) and `--env prod`. ADOPS_SERVER_DIR is read from the prod environment's variables.

phases.rationale: The generated workflows only work after manual GitHub and Server setup that adops cannot do for the user without repo-admin credentials. The fork-approval setting is the real security boundary for self-hosted runners. Without written steps, a user cannot turn Promotion on safely. The decisions behind the workflows (self-hosted runner per Server, Fork PR policy, push instead of Git pull) are written here, next to the guide that explains them, so the workflow phases stay about YAML generation and the records are reviewed together on their own grounds.
